newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Local borrowing covers less of Israel budget gap.
newsitem.headline: Local borrowing covers less of Israel budget gap.

text.p: The government financed only 58 percent of its domestic deficit by borrowing in local capital markets in the first 10 months of the year, compared with 66 percent in all of 1995, the Bank of Israel said on Wednesday.
The rest of the deficit was financed mainly by foreign currency loans and by drawing on deposits held by the government in the Bank of Israel.
In 1995, foreign currency loans and central bank deposits financed less than 25 percent of the domestic deficit.

The central bank attributed the trend at least in part to the growing cost of domestic borrowing. The average rate of interest on inflation-index Treasury bonds rose to about five percent this year from 4.5 percent in 1995 and 3.3 percent in 1994.
In the August-October period, when bond market yields peaked, the government did not borrow at all in the domestic capital market.
The government raised a net 5.9 billion shekels by issuing bonds in the first 10 months, 300 million shekels from privatisation and 4.4 billion shekels through monetary injections.
Israel's total deficit in the first 10 months of 1996 was 10.3 billion shekels, including credits granted by the government, according to the Bank of Israel.
